newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Somali faction leaders agree ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Somali faction leaders agree ceasefire.

text.p: Somalia's two most powerful faction leaders, Hussein Aideed and Ali Mahdi Mohamed, agreed on Monday to a ceasefire in the anarchic Horn of Africa nation after three hours of face-to-face talks.

The two leaders hugged each other and exchanged traditional Somali kisses before going into closed-door talks at a hotel along Mogadishu's Greenline, which separates the divided city into the north controlled by Ali Mahdi and the south by Aideed.
This was the second agreement by the two leaders since former U.S. marine Aideed succeeded his late father, warlord Mohamed Farah Aideed whose forces humbled American troops in Somalia.
Both faction leaders lay claim to the presidency of the broken Moslem nation.

A statement issued at the end of the talks said the two arch-rivals had agreed to a ceasefire throughout the territories they control. They also agreed to form a joint police force to monitor the ceasefire and to enforce the removal of checkpoints.
"They have agreed to a ceasefire. They also agreed to remove all checkpoints and to form a joint police force," an official said, quoting the statement.

The two Somali leaders also agreed to set up a committee to look into the possibility of reopening the Mogadishu port and airport, closed since 1995 because of feuds between the two factions over finances and control.

In October the two factions met in the Kenyan capital and agreed to end hostilities in their devastated country. But the accord led to nowhere. There was no face-to-face meeting between the two leaders at the Nairobi talks.
Aideed is a 34-year old former U.S. marine who took over from the elder Aideed following his death in Mogadishu on August 1 last year.
Aideed like his father was elected president of Somalia by supporters and heads a government. But it has not received international recognition and is rejected by Ali Mahdi and other faction leaders.
Ali Mahdi claims to head the biggest clan network in Somalia and counts on millionaire financier, Hassan Ali Osman Atto, among his allies.

Somalia has been without central authority since 1991 after rebels overthrew late president Mohamed Siad Barre. But they soon turned their guns on each other in vicious fighting which killed thousands and laid waste to Somalia.

A U.S. led U.N. intervention force of some 35,000 troops failed to restore law and order in Somalia and had to pull out after it got entangled in battles with Aideed's forces in which American servicemen were killed and captured.
The Somalis have signed numerous peace accords since 1991 but all have failed to return the country, one of the poorest on the continent of Africa, to normality.
In some parts of Somalia authority oftens means a few teenage kids armed with automatic rifles.
